issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one. 'Being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/self-directed trauma context that is not supported anywhere else in the profile and is hard to reconcile with bereavement/trauma-to-loved-one as the index trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items do not form a coherent theme. 'Talking about the future' could fit grief-related loss, but 'incomprehensible chatter' and especially 'being looked at sexually' point toward very different trauma contexts, making the trigger profile internally inconsistent for a single index trauma.

vignette:
Kofi Mensah is a 63-year-old Ghanaian-American journalist, married for thirty-one years, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 49 following a traumatic event involving his youngest son, Kwame, who suffered a catastrophic stroke eighteen months ago at the age of thirty-four. Kofi was present in the hospital room when the medical team attempted to stabilise Kwame, and he recalls standing at the foot of the bed as monitors alarmed and staff spoke rapidly across one another in the dense, overlapping shorthand of a resuscitation effort - words that blurred into a wall of sound he could not parse, could not hold onto, could not answer. What he does remember with terrible precision is the taste in his mouth at that moment: the metallic bitterness of the coffee he had been drinking when his daughter-in-law called, a taste that had followed him into the hospital and lodged itself in the back of his throat as the scene unfolded. Kwame survived, but with significant cognitive impairment, and Kofi has never fully left that room.

In the months that followed, Kofi found that the memory of what happened resisted the very tools his profession had given him. He is a man who has spent four decades finding the precise word for difficult things - conflict, grief, injustice - and yet when he attempts to describe what he witnessed, the thread dissolves. He knows what happened. The knowledge sits in him like a stone. But when he opens his mouth to give it shape, the language fails to arrive, and he trails into silence, sometimes mid-sentence, in a way that disturbs him deeply. He has tried to write it down for himself, privately, and the same thing happens on the page: a beginning, and then nothing. He has come to believe that this failure is not incidental, that it means something irreparable occurred in him that night, something that cannot be communicated and therefore cannot be shared or relieved.

His triggers are specific and, in the context of his life as a journalist, unavoidable. Kofi covers human interest and social affairs for a regional outlet, and his work regularly places him in conversations about loss - interviews with families who have experienced bereavement, features on grief and ageing, panel discussions about mortality and legacy. When a source begins to talk about losing a loved one, or when a colleague in an editorial meeting speaks about someone's death, Kofi feels the room shift. The metallic taste returns first, rising at the back of his palate before the images follow - the monitors, the voices, the particular angle of Kwame's face turned away from him. What he finds most destabilising, however, is the sound of incomprehensible chatter: overlapping voices, a crowded newsroom, a busy restaurant where multiple conversations merge into unintelligible noise. That texture of sound - language that cannot be decoded - pulls him back with a force that surprises him each time, flooding him with the sensory residue of that hospital room before he has had time to prepare. The taste comes with it, vivid and unwanted, and for a few seconds he is no longer at his desk or across from an interview subject but standing at the foot of Kwame's bed, unable to understand what is being said and unable to do anything at all.

Conversations about the future carry their own weight. When his wife speaks hopefully about retirement plans, or when friends discuss what the grandchildren will be like, Kofi goes quiet in a way his wife has begun to notice and name. He cannot orient himself toward a future that once felt continuous and now feels conditional in ways he cannot articulate.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a profile assignment - a piece about a family navigating a loved one's acquired brain injury - that he accepted and then could not write. He sat with the transcript for three weeks and produced nothing. His editor asked questions he could not answer honestly. He is most afraid, he says, that the words will never come back. What he hopes, more quietly, is that someone might be able to help him finish the sentence he has been trying to complete for eighteen months.
